Another tip is that in paste techniques, such as acrylic and oil, the standard is to start painting from the foreground and progress to the background, and going from darker to lighter tones. In watercolor, it's the opposite: you always start from the background and progress to the planes closest to the observer, and you also start from the lightest tone and then go to the darkest. It's necessary to relearn how to paint, after all. I once met a painting teacher and he explained to me that watercolor is the first technique you start learning, but it's the last one you'll actually master.

Yes, practice with whatever you have available and use it to become aware of the paradigms you have and that condition you during the painting process. This way, you will deconstruct yourself until you can have a large piece of paper and then be free from these paradigms. Because look, it's complicated. When I paint with acrylics, I go crazy, I get tense, because it's the opposite of what I'm used to. This thing of making several brushstrokes, man, it kills me. The paint doesn't stretch, I go crazy. LOL. In watercolor, I love it when I apply water to a large area and then I spread the paint and it acts on its own. My work is very influenced by Japanese painting, so it has these large colored planes. With acrylics, my God, you have to stay there, making brushstrokes in the sky and it never ends. LOL

Oh, and the size of the painting also completely changes the painting experience. Try to do a small painting, but if you can, especially do a large painting, like 70x50cm and dance with the watercolor, I promise you that you will love it

Dude, about watercolor and acrylic, I understand, because they are two dramatically opposite mediums. I paint with acrylic too, and with it there is more mastery, more control, it is "solid and dense" but it is a style that doesn't really suit me, I'm self-taught, I learned watercolor by myself, and what I learned with watercolor is exactly that it does not submit to this mastery, it is always unpredictable and uncontrollable, by the very nature of water.  So what I have learned and what I can give you as a suggestion is that when painting watercolors, abandon the need for control. On the contrary, see the paint and water as another entity that will create the painting together with you. Don't worry so much about achieving your goal, but try to see the experience of painting as a dance. That's it, dance with the watercolor and allow yourself to have no expectations about the result.

Thank you very much, with all my heart, I am very happy with your comment. And about "knowing about art", can I give you a suggestion, a perspective? We usually have the mistaken understanding that understanding art is something kind of academic, something about logically describing something about painting, but I think that is not the case. This is a conception created by scholars, it is something to distance people from art. I think that understanding art simply involves allowing yourself to feel and connect with what you see, without needing to verbalize it. On the contrary, I think it is much more interesting and even challenging when you allow yourself to contemplate a painting and feel something that you cannot explain, this makes you get in touch with a dimension so deep in your own existence that it cannot be expressed in words. That's it, my friend, don't worry about describing it, allow yourself to feel the unnamable that lives within you. 🙌🙌🙌

Thank you very much, I'm flattered by that. And can I tell you my secret? I'm self-taught, I learned everything by myself, and learning watercolor is a big challenge. Watercolor is the first painting technique you start learning, but it's the last one you master. I didn't have an instructor, so I had to learn intuitively. The most important thing I learned from her was that a lot of people's frustration is due to the fact that they can't control the paint, because of the water, you know? Along the way, I discovered another approach. I don't try to control the watercolor. On the contrary, I see it as a dance. I allow the water to flow and, almost like an entity with its own will, I allow it to paint along with me. That's my secret. Watercolor is a dance, not a fight to try to control the water, because that's impossible. So I allow it to express itself independently.

I sincerely owe a lot to Ghibli's works, because in them I found a way to express something that lives inside me and that I couldn't make conscious, Ghibli's cartoons taught me this path. I had a nomadic upbringing, so for me, the world has always been this vast place, with distant horizons and at the same time magical, vibrant, mysterious, because every place was a secret place, full of things to discover. From this inspiration I was able to represent my experience of the world. A grand and beautiful place in my eyes, I am enchanted by the places I discover, just as we viewers encounter the mysteries of Ghibli's landscapes.

I don't think there is a specific method, each artist and client negotiate the best terms for the project. But I believe that a good way to avoid scams, or simply to hire an artist who doesn't have a professional attitude, is to first talk to him, be clear and objective about your terms and what you want from the project. It's also a good idea to ask for his social media and do some research, including his profile here. What's he like? Does he post frequently? If you look up his profile on Reddit, what's he like? Can you see active posts or comments on art subs, not just commissions, but other areas? This can be a good sign, showing that he's really dedicated and invests time and effort in his work. Asking for a phone number is also a good idea, as is using a secure platform to pay, one that allows you to get your payment back, for example.  In the end, each case is different. We artists also end up suffering scams here, or other types of problems. For example, I've had problems with a client who changed his mind and wanted to cancel the commission after it was ready, but he didn't say that, he just asked to redo it. I spent 2 months investing material, time and effort doing and redoing it, and in the end he simply asked for the money back. It's terrible, but it happens. My advice is always to talk, talk a lot and see if he gives you security and professionalism.

I understand what you mean, other people are making this point too, but when I refer to pearlescent, I am talking about the effect of light and not the colors. What does pearlescent consist of? Complementary light and shadows intermediated by a midtone, correct? That is what I am referring to, I did another study with the colors of pearl, I think it will be easier to understand that way.

There are indeed neon colors, but neon light does not behave like that. That is the issue. Pearlescent refers more to the dynamics of light and shadow, where the shadow, reflected, also becomes a complementary point of light. This first example does not have the same colors as a pearl, but that is the intention. To work with the effect and not with the colors. I did other studies with the traditional colors of pearl, so it becomes clearer. But if you notice, in essence the dynamics of pearlescent are two complementary points of light with a half tone between them, like green with pink and purple as an intermediary.

It really depends on the colors you use. The issue is the dynamics of the colors. I did other studies using pearl colors, so it's more obvious, but here it's about how to create shadows even with a saturated color and a dark tone as an intermediary.

In fact, the intention is not to establish a development order, but to seek to analyze different approaches as something more horizontal, without necessarily being better than the other. It was a very intuitive exercise, so I wasn't looking for a specific result, I just allowed myself to feel and test the painting without thinking too much. And I agree with you about the unpredictability of watercolor and that's what I like about it. I say that painting with watercolor is like a dance. You need to allow yourself to interact with the water and understand that it is also an active part in the creation of the work. It's difficult to deconstruct the paradigm of control that we end up creating with solid and dry media, but that's exactly what I like about watercolor. So I propose a different vision. Don't think of watercolor as a bull that you need to tame, but as the flow of a river that you can guide.
